answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
• Consequential accounting methods can serve as helpful tools to analyze the system-wide emissions impacts of projects or interventions; however, they can suffer from serious technical challenges and result in unintended consequences for investments in the voluntary clean energy market.
• GHG Protocol’s Public Consultation Draft for Consequential Electricity Sector Emissions Impact (Draft) notes that additionality is a key component of consequential accounting methods. According to the Draft, projects that can demonstrate additionality—wherein the project scenario differs from a baseline scenario—are considered to reduce system-wide emissions. Yet, a key methodological challenge is how a baseline is established, and which projects are deemed eligible to be analyzed in a project scenario. If additionality rules narrowly consider only certain kinds of projects as eligible under the project scenario (e.g., only a brand-new solar project) and include all existing facilities in the baseline—no matter their performance, role in grid decarbonization, or economic needs—then these stringent rules can unnecessarily limit the number of recognized GHG reductions and in some cases exclude projects that are additional and highly desirable.
• In the U.S., hydropower, including pumped storage hydropower, serves as a case in point. Hydropower has unique grid attributes that are essential for grid decarbonization. Hydropower can displace fossil-fuel-based generation, given its ability to operate at all hours of the day and ramp up when wind and solar are unavailable. Hydropower is also routinely called upon for its ancillary services including black start capabilities, regulation, and spinning reserves (see, https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2021/01/f82/us-hydropower-market-report-full-2021.pdf). Despite hydropower’s essential contribution to advancing grid decarbonization, flexibility, and reliability, this resource is often excluded under narrow definitions of additionality (e.g., when only new resources count) since a large number of facilities in the existing U.S. fleet are multi-decade old. This narrow view of additionality ignores the capital-intensive nature of hydropower: facilities require long payback periods for their initial capital investment and continue to need additional investments throughout their life for their upkeep, maintenance, refurbishment, and repowering (see, https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87470.pdf; https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2021/01/f82/us-hydropower-market-report-full-2021.pdf; https://atb.nrel.gov/electricity/2024/hydropower). The U.S. has both regulated and deregulated electricity markets that affect ownership structures of hydropower projects and their ability to access necessary investments. Simply slating existing resources, such as hydropower, in a baseline scenario disregards their ongoing investment needs at best and, at worst, assumes their continued operation despite economic realities—with particularly detrimental outcomes for independently owned projects in deregulated markets. This treatment for existing hydropower could inadvertently chill necessary investment in this strategic resource at a critical point in time: 40% of the U.S. non-federal hydro fleet is coming up for relicensing in the next few years and projects will likely need new investments to upgrade facilities and extend the life of assets.
• The pitfalls outlined in the aforementioned example underscore the need for a careful development of additionality rules in the consequential accounting method. As a rule of thumb, consequential accounting should not disincentivize investments in renewable resources at a time when we need every electron to achieve societal decarbonization goals.
• Broadly, consequential accounting should complement attributional accounting and not replace it.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
•Hydropower facilities, like all energy systems, can emit greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions over their entire lifecycle (See https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1364032111001924; https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/17/13/5794)
•Human-made reservoirs can emit GHGs, and for hydropower facilities with a reservoir— regardless of whether hydropower generation is the primary purpose of the reservoir—the creation and unique characteristics of the reservoir along with its ongoing operation play a key role in influencing the overall rate of GHG emissions from individual facilities (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2005GB002457; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1364032122003161). In other words, hydropower facilities with a reservoir may have not only one-time secondary effects (i.e., GHG emissions that occur during the construction, installation, and decommissioning or a project), but also ongoing secondary effects resulting from the operation of the water reservoir. Reservoirs can also serve as GHG emission sinks.
•Individual reservoir characteristics, such as the age, location, size, and morphology of the water reservoir, operational patterns [e.g., run-of-river, storage/peaking], water quality and stratification in the reservoir, external environmental factors etc. can all affect the rate and pathways of GHG emissions from water reservoirs. (See, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32801383/; https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/17/13/5794)
•Estimating GHG emissions from water reservoirs is methodologically challenging given the uncertainty and strong spatial and temporal variability in GHG emissions at individual reservoirs, including those with hydropower facilities (See, https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/17/13/5794 for a synthesis of the latest advancements in tools and methodologies in estimating GHGs at reservoirs).
• Recognizing the potential for the release of GHG emissions at water reservoirs, specifically those with hydropower generation, the GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removal Guidance development process will include guidance on calculating methane (CH4) emissions from reservoirs and other flooded lands. A Draft of the Guidance that was released in 2022. This draft notes that “[c]ompanies that purchase electricity from hydropower [should] report CH4 emissions from the hydropower reservoirs used to generate electricity as scope 2 emissions.” Final guidance is expected to be released at the end of January 2026.
• Given the hydropower and water reservoir-specific context discussed above, it is important to consider the secondary effects of projects in addition to primary effects. It is worth noting that LIHI is using the term secondary effects for ongoing emissions from reservoir operations since the GHG Protocol’s Consequential Accounting Public Consultation document notes that “[f]or renewable energy generation the project scenario Primary Effect emissions are usually zero," meaning the “Primary Effects” term would consider hydropower’s emission rate as zero. If GHG Procotol intended to include direct operational emissions in its estimation of Primary Effects, then hydropower reservoir emissions—especially degassing emissions from turbine operations—would factor into the calculation of Primary Effects.
• The Consequential Accounting Guidance can look to the Land Sector & Removal Guidance for methodologies to estimate GHG emissions (notably methane) from reservoirs associated with hydropower facilities. If reservoirs serve multiple purposes in addition to hydropower generation (e.g., water supply, flood control), additional considerations would be needed to appropriately attribute emissions to the function of electricity generation (see examples of allocation methods here, https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/64f9d0036cb97160cc26feba/64f9d0036cb97160cc270fe1_g-res_technical_document_v2.1.pdf).

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
• Emissions impacts of electricity projects should be calculated and reported each reporting year since the magnitude of emissions from hydropower projects, specifically with water reservoirs, can vary each year over the life of a project.
• Existing research suggests that GHG emissions from water reservoirs may vary over the life of a project. Some studies have found that reservoirs, including those with hydropower facilities, may have higher GHG emissions in the first few years after they are newly constructed (See, https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo1211). Others have found that while carbon dioxide emissions have been declining as reservoirs age, methane emissions continue to rise (See, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-022-01004-2). Reservoirs can also serve as GHG emission sinks.
• Consequently, annual reporting can help determine the trends in emissions impacts from a project on a year-over-year basis. This information in turn can help inform strategies to mitigate emissions.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
• Majority of the listed additionality tests would not be feasible for the U.S. hydropower fleet despite its essential contribution to advancing grid decarbonization, flexibility, and reliability.
• For example, U.S. hydropower projects would have great difficulty meeting the timing test or the financial tests as proposed since majority of the projects are currently operational. The narrow perspective of these tests disregards the capital-intensive nature and economic reality of hydropower projects, and misunderstands how projects operate in practice. Hydropower facilities require long payback periods for their initial capital investment and continue to have ongoing maintenance and repowering expenses throughout their life (see, https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87470.pdf; https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2021/01/f82/us-hydropower-market-report-full-2021.pdf; https://atb.nrel.gov/electricity/2024/hydropower). LIHI Certified® projects often require investments for necessary environmental and sustainability measures. The timing test notes that if a project was already planned or under construction before an incentive was available (e.g., tax credit), then the facility would fail the test. Most of the existing hydropower projects in the U.S. would fail to meet this simplistic timing test; yet the reality is that incentives are but one part of a capital stack for existing projects, and they are critically necessary to keep projects operational and online. In other words, simply because a hydropower project is already built does not mean that it does not need continued investment to prevent decommissioning or license surrender [from 2010 to 2022 alone, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued 68 surrenders for hydropower licenses (and exemptions) with a combined capacity of 322 MW, and the most frequently reason cited for surrender was economic infeasibility, see https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2023-09/U.S.%20Hydropower%20Market%20Report%202023%20Edition.pdf]. Moreover, hydropower projects often perform repowering and upgrades on a turbine level, not project level. So, simply the pre-existence of a project for a timing perspective would fail to qualify turbine-level upgrades as additional even though the upgrades would in fact result in extending the life of the project as a whole. When it comes to the financial test, if the test is solely looking at a single contract (e.g., PPA) to assess whether that contact turns a project from being financially unattractive to attractive, then that too fails to acknowledge that hydropower projects often require multiple offtakes (and price premiums) across regions and diverse revenue streams to stay operational—a single investment alone would likely not change the financial outlook of a project and would be an improper way to assess additionality.
• With 40% of the hydropower fleet in the U.S. coming up for relicensing in the next few years and policy headwinds for renewable development, region and technology-specific considerations are necessary in crafting additionality tests to prevent unintentional chilling of investments in the hydropower fleet and renewables more broadly (see examples of additionality considerations for hydropower in response to question 32).

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text:
• Different additionality tests are necessary for the hydropower fleet in the United States since the currently proposed tests fail to capture the unique economic and operational considerations of this fleet.
• Some recommended approaches for assessing additionality as it relates to the U.S. hydropower fleet include: 1. Relicensing—40% of the U.S. non-federal hydropower fleet is coming up for relicensing in the next few years. Relicensed projects should be considered to have new commissioning dates given that significant new investments will likely be made to upgrade or overhaul facilities; 2. Repowering/turbine upgrades—Upgrades at U.S. hydropower facilities rarely occur at the project-level and often focus on individual generators. Repowering and/or turbine upgrades can result in meaningful improvements in generator performance and capacity. Any investments or upgrades at the turbine-level should be considered additional; 3. LIHI Certification—LIHI runs United States’ only science-based program to certify Low Impact hydropower facilities (See, https://lowimpacthydro.org/certification-program/). LIHI Certified® facilities often make significant new investments in their facilities in the process of certification. Regardless of a dam’s age (and especially for multi-decade old dams), these investments help improve the environmental performance of hydropower projects and enhance power generation outcomes. LIHI Certification also improves a projects’ ability to attract further funding and market incentives that can make a difference in whether a project chooses to remain operational and undergo relicensing (e.g., Brookfield’s Holtwood Project in Pennsylvania is LIHI Certified®. The world’s largest $3 billion framework agreement for the procurement of hydropower between Google and Brookfield was for Holtwood and one other project. Brookfield notes that Google’s investment will allow the projects to be relicensed, overhauled, or upgraded to extend the asset’s useful life and continue adding power to the grid. See, https://bam.brookfield.com/press-releases/brookfield-and-google-sign-hydro-framework-agreement-deliver-3000-mw-homegrown).

audit_basis: Own Q29 text: 'LIHI Certified(R) projects often require investments for necessary environmental and sustainability measures' - it operates a hydropower certification programme.
